rss.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
rss.summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. rss.title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
rss.summary: Google launches Humanity’s First Exam to test LLM reliability across 544 prompts.
rss.text_excerpt: Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard , or read our technical report . To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

rss.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
rss.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

rss.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
rss.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. rss.summary: See how two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to find potential exoplanets in public data from NASA’s Kepler and TESS space telescopes.
rss.text_excerpt:
Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system ⁠ (opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers. Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope ⁠ (opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars. Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission. One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. rss.summary: November 23, 2026 — Nvidia reinstates its founder, and OpenAI publishes its internal loss curve and proposes a shared training limit.
rss.text_excerpt:
November 23, 2026 — Nvidia reinstates its founder, and OpenAI publishes its internal loss curve and proposes a shared training limit. Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly . The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. rss.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
rss.summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. rss.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
rss.summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. rss.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
rss.text_excerpt:
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. # Corvid **Build the whole application — interface, backend and AI — in one language, where people and AI agents use the same typed actions.** Corvid is a general-purpose programming language. A small app takes a few lines, and a team can build a large AI application at full scale from the first day with the same grammar, types and tools. Anything you build on the backend and AI side with Python or TypeScript and their libraries is meant to be buildable in Corvid, through built-in features or typed interoperability. > Corvid is pre-1.0 and under active development. This page shows only what runs today and says plainly what is still being built. The [platform plan](docs/proposals/corvid-platform-plan.md) describes what comes next. ## Why one language for the interface, backend and AI Today one feature is split across a database, a backend in one language, a frontend in another and an AI layer added on top, each with its own types, validation and permissions, kept in step by hand. Corvid puts them in one program that one compiler understands: - **One definition, everywhere.** A type or a table is declared once and used by the database, the backend, the interface and the AI. Rename a field and the compiler points at every place that uses it, instead of a user finding the break in production. - **The API keeps itself in sync.** The backend publishes a typed contract, and the TypeScript client and the Swift, Kotlin and Python SDKs are generated from it, so a client cannot drift from the server. - **People and AI use the same actions.** A button and an assistant can run the same handler. **经验留在公司。** 服务器每晚把所有人当天的 AI 对话和公司文档整理进知识库，谁能搜到什么按人和部门控制。 基于 [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)（`dsh`），按公司场景打了补丁。MIT 许可，第三方部分见 [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md)。 ## 长什么样 | 任务 | 同事 | 人员 | | --- | --- | --- | | ![任务](docs/screenshots/04-tasks.jpg) | ![同事](docs/screenshots/02-colleagues.jpg) | ![人员](docs/screenshots/03-personnel.jpg) | | 任务卡有状态和负责人，点开就带着任务开工 | 谁在线、角色、最后登录、近七日用量 | 按部门管花名册，改角色、停用、吊销令牌 | 最上面那张是一段真实对话：销售表是编的，回答由模型生成。截图里的人名、任务和用量都是演示数据。每个界面的详细说明见 [项目讲解](docs/BRIEF.zh.md#打开之后是什么)。 ## 适合谁 | 适合 | 不适合 | | --- | --- | | 10–50 人，在同一个办公室局域网，有一台能常开的 Windows 电脑当服务器 | 想要托管 SaaS，或者服务器要跑在 Linux / Docker 上（目前服务器只支持 Windows） | | 想让每个人的 AI 在自己电脑上真的把活干了，钥匙、额度和公司盘由公司统一管 | 只想要一个聊天界面，或者几千份文档的问答门户（见下面的对比） | | 中文办公文档：Word / Excel / PowerPoint、WPS、PDF、扫描件 | 需要按意思搜索（搜「费用核销」找到「报销」）：目前是关键词检索（BM25），没有向量库 | | 现场有人在出问题时能看懂 PowerShell 和 Node | 需要 AD / LDAP / SSO 登录（目前账号是 TDH 自己的花名册） | ## 安装 ### 第一步：装服务器（一台 Windows，装一次） 需要 Windows 10/11 或 Windows Server、管理员权限，事先装好 Git（含 Git LFS）、Node 22+、Python 3。系统自带的 Windows PowerShell 就够用。 ```powershell git clone https://github.com/398894496-arch/TDHarness.git cd TDHarness git lfs pull powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\setup-all.ps1 ``` 看到 `SITE_INSTALL_OK=1`、`LOGIN_PROVE_OK=1`、`GUI_PROVE_OK=1`、`PLANT_CLIENT_OK=1` 就是装好了。这一条命令装出：登录、种子管理员、花名册、模型网关、知识库和每晚的整理任务、下载页，以及按这台服务器编译好的 Windows 和 Mac 客户端。 **默认管理员账号是 `tdh`，初始密码每次安装随机生成**：装机结束时显示在 `DEFAULT_PASSWORD=` 这一行，也存在服务器的 `D:\dsh\runt

github.description: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) —— DeepSeek AI 开源的 Agent 智能体框架，群晖 Synology DSM / 飞牛 fnOS NAS 原生打包（SPK/FPK），无需 Docker，开箱即用。Web UI 管理、多模型、内置反向代理与局域网安全限制。
github.text_excerpt:
# DeepSeekHarness-NAS DeepSeek Harness（dsh）的 NAS 适配包：群晖 DSM `.spk` / 飞牛 fnOS `.fpk`，在 NAS 原生运行，无需容器。 ## 功能 | 功能 | 做什么 | 入口 | |---|---|---| | 套件安装 | 群晖装 spk、飞牛装 fpk，装完即用 | 套件中心 | | Web UI | 多模型配置、自定义 OpenAI 兼容端点 | `http://<NAS-IP>:30800`（spk）/ `:3080`（fpk） | | 反向代理 | 反代端口对外，dsh 原生端口仅本机 | `http://<NAS-IP>:<反代端口>` | | 门户免密 | 套件图标打开带 token，认证后免密 | DSM/fnOS 桌面图标 | | 局域网限制 | 公网 IP 一律 403 提示页 | 内置，无需配置 | | 命令行 `dsh` / `pnpm` | 装完 SSH 直接敲，无需进套件目录 | `/usr/bin/dsh`、`/usr/bin/pnpm` | | 自动构建发布 | 官方更新自动对齐构建，发 Release 双产物 | GitHub Actions | | 架构参数化 | 同一脚本出 x86_64 / arm64 包 | `build/config/build-config.yaml` 的 `defaults.arch` | ## 访问地址与端口 | 平台 | 反代端口（唯一入口） | dsh 原生端口（仅本机） | 容器页端口 | |---|---|---|---| | 群晖 DSM（spk） | 30800 | 30801 | 30802 | | 飞牛 fnOS（fpk） | 3080 | 3081 | 3082 | 权威值在 `build/config/build-config.yaml` 的 `defaults` / `spk` / `fpk` 三段；改端口只改这里。 ### 登录（OAuth）需要回环访问 浏览器登录只接受回环来源（`127.0.0.1` / `localhost` / `[::1]`）。用 SSH 本地转发，端口由脚本从目标机读取；建好后在 `http://127.0.0.1:<端口>` 登录。不需要登录时用 API Key。 ```bash scripts/connect-local.sh <NAS-IP> # Linux / macOS；本机端口被占用时加 LOCAL_PORT=31800 scripts/connect-local.bat # Windows：双击后按提示输入 NAS 地址 ``` ## 安装与卸载 - 群晖：套件中心 → 手动安装 → 选 `.spk`（DSM 7.0-40851 起，x86_64）；飞牛：应用中心 → 手动安装 → 选 `.fpk`（fnOS 1.1.0 起）。 - 安装向导可留空端口（用打包默认）；卸载向导默认**保留数据**，选「彻底删除」才清数据；卸载走 Web UI（命令行会被平台拒绝）。 - 回退旧版：Web UI 卸载（保持默认「保留数据」）→ 装旧版包 → 直接启动。数据按版本目录隔离，各版本用各自的配置与会话。 ### 从套件源安装（可自动更新） 套件中心里显示已安装版本、最新在线版本与更新日志，可直接点「更新」；把包作为「套件来源」加进去后，套件中心会按版本比较提示更新。 ```bash # 起一个本地套件源（任意能访问 GitHub 的机器），再把地址加进 套件中心 → 设置 → 套件来源 python3 scripts/pkg-source.py --repo EIGHTfs/DeepSeekHarness-NAS --port 8899 # x86_64：http://<该机器IP>:8899/index-x86_64.json # armv8 ：http://<该机器IP>:8899/index-armv8.json ``` ![套件中心里从本地套件源安装后的效果](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EIGHTfs/DeepSeekHarness-NAS/main/docs/images/package-source-in-center.jpg) ## 常用操作（start.sh） ```bash ./start.sh start # 启动（拉起 dsh → 反代 → 容器页 → 校验端口） ./start.sh stop # 停止；卸载流程下输出「已卸载」 ./start.sh restart # 重启（未启动时相当于 start） ./start.sh status # 查状态：0=运行中，3=未运行 ./start.sh fix-deps # 启动报缺包时的补齐兜底 ./start.sh gen-portal --token # 重新生成门户入口并写入当次 token ``` ```bash synopkg start DeepSeekHarness-NAS # 群晖启停（stop/restart/status 同名） appcenter-cli start DeepSeekHarness-NAS # 飞牛启停（stop/status/check 同名） ``` ## 数据目录与版本隔离 数据按版本隔离：`<平台应用数据目录>/<版本>/`（群晖为 `/volume1/@appdata/<包名>/<版本>/`），内含 `.dsh/`（即 `DSH_HOME`）、`ports`、日志与 PID。升级、回退、并存各用各的目录，互不覆盖；卸载默认保留，`--delete-data` 才删
